topStories.headline: SCRAP Opens Permanent Home in Bayview, Doubling Its Space After 50 Years
topStories.dek: The beloved creative-reuse nonprofit celebrated its grand opening at 141 Industrial St. on Saturday, Aug. 15, securing its first-ever owned building.
topStories.body:
After half a century of renting space from the San Francisco Unified School District, SCRAP — the Scroungers' Center for Reusable Art Parts — has moved into a permanent home it now owns. The nonprofit held its grand opening at 141 Industrial Street in the Bayview on Saturday, August 15, with a tree-planting ceremony, ribbon-cutting, free hands-on workshops, and refreshments. The new building, purchased for a reported $5.3 million after the previous owner went into foreclosure, gives SCRAP nearly 26,000 square feet — roughly double its previous footprint at 2150 Newcomb Ave.

SCRAP's former warehouse was leased from SFUSD for 25 years, but the school district needed the building to convert it into its central kitchen hub. The move had been years in the making, and for a time the nonprofit's future was uncertain. The new building on Industrial Street — previously owned by Calvary Hill Community Church, which will remain as an upstairs tenant — is SCRAP's first permanent home in its history.

The new facility adds dedicated workshop space on-site for the first time, allowing for expanded bookbinding, basket-making, and community art sessions that had been constrained by the old single-room layout. SCRAP's educational programs, which serve more than 45,000 people in the Bayview annually and have diverted over 250 tons of material from the waste stream, will continue without interruption. Workshops at partner venues including SFMOMA and SF Public Libraries also continue on their regular schedule.

"This building is core to creating the foundation for San Francisco's creative future," said executive director Terry Kochanski, according to Mission Local. SCRAP's signature hand-drawn blue Sharpie signage and charmingly mislabeled containers will make the move with the organization.

topStories.headline: Residents and Supervisor Push Back on Data Centers Planned Near Bayview and Visitacion Valley
topStories.dek: Two proposed surveillance data centers near Bayview–Hunters Point and Visitacion Valley are raising alarms over pollution, water use, and a lack of community input.
topStories.body:
Two planned data centers near Bayview–Hunters Point and Visitacion Valley are drawing fierce opposition from residents and elected officials who say the projects moved forward without adequate community engagement. The San Francisco Bay View reports that journalist JR Valrey has documented the proposals, which raise concerns about cumulative pollution burdens, high water consumption, and neighborhood impacts in an area already classified as one of the most environmentally burdened communities in California.

District 10 Supervisor Shamann Walton has indicated that the projects advanced without community input and that the situation may prompt legislative action. The concerns echo longstanding environmental justice fights in Bayview–Hunters Point, a predominantly Black, Latine, and Asian American Pacific Islander neighborhood where nearly 38 percent of land is zoned for industrial use — compared to about 7 percent citywide — and where residents already face disproportionate exposures to diesel truck traffic, the Hunters Point Naval Shipyard Superfund site, and emissions from industrial facilities.

Data centers have become a growing flashpoint in environmental justice communities nationally. Advocates argue the facilities' intensive power and water demands compound existing pollution burdens, while developers and some city officials point to job creation and economic development benefits. The Bay Area Air Quality Management District has been engaged in a multi-year Community Emissions Reduction Plan process for the Bayview–Hunters Point area under California's AB 617 law, holding regular community steering committee meetings at the Southeast Community Center.

topStories.headline: Crocker Amazon Park Battle Heats Up as Opponents Schedule Community Rallies This Month
topStories.dek: The Keep Crocker Real coalition has organized back-to-back community events in August as the controversial $50 million Giants-backed turf renovation heads toward a Board of Supervisors vote.
topStories.body:
The fight over the future of Crocker Amazon Park in the Excelsior is entering a critical phase, with opponents of a planned $50 million artificial-turf ballfield complex scheduling two community events this month ahead of a key City Hall hearing. The advocacy group Keep Crocker Real has organized a community gathering at the Hummingbird Farm within Crocker Amazon Park on Friday, August 22 from 2–5 p.m., and a public hearing at City Hall, Room 408, on Monday, August 24 at 5 p.m.

The Recreation and Park Commission unanimously voted in April to recommend that the Board of Supervisors accept a $28 million grant from the San Francisco Giants — to be combined with $22 million in city funds — for the renovation. The plan calls for five artificial turf baseball diamonds, covered batting cages, upgraded lighting, and new restrooms, with the fields to be named the Willie Mays Fields of Champions in honor of the late baseball legend. City planners say the project could expand access to safe play by up to 10,000 additional hours per year.

Opponents, including Keep Crocker Real and neighboring Pacific Islander community members, argue the design would remove up to 124 trees, replace natural open space with fenced synthetic turf, and eliminate the park's current use for Samoan cricket, movie nights, and large community gatherings. District 11 Supervisor Chyanne Chen has called for greater community input, saying the renovation "can't come at the expense of the needs of our neighborhood park users," according to Mission Local. Keep Crocker Real has also filed formal CEQA comments asking the Planning Department to require a full Environmental Impact Report.

The project's prospective construction start date is listed as 2027–2028, meaning the Board of Supervisors vote in the coming months will be a pivotal moment for both sides of the debate.

events.title: Keep Crocker Real Community Gathering at Hummingbird Farm
events.location: Hummingbird Farm at Crocker Amazon Park, near 1669 Geneva Ave, Crocker Amazon
events.description: Community members opposed to the artificial-turf renovation plan will gather at the Hummingbird Farm inside Crocker Amazon Park. Residents are encouraged to share their vision for the park ahead of the City Hall hearing on August 24.

events.title: Sunday Streets Bayview
events.location: Lane Street between Thomas and Underwood Avenues, Bayview
events.description: San Francisco's open streets program returns to the Bayview for a free, car-free day of live music, a Kids Zone hosted by the Bayview YMCA, health resources, and community activities. SFMTA's Bayview Community Pathway team will also be on-site to gather feedback on the neighborhood's planned protected bikeway.

events.title: Crocker Amazon Park Renovation Public Hearing — City Hall
events.description: A public hearing on the proposed $50 million Crocker Amazon Park baseball complex renovation, backed by the SF Giants. Community members are invited to tell decision-makers what kind of park they want.

events.title: Visitacion Valley Night Market — Inaugural Edition
events.location: Leland Avenue between Bayshore & Peabody, Visitacion Valley
events.description: The first-ever Visitacion Valley Night Market takes over Leland Avenue with free admission, food vendors, local shopping, live music by DJ Cilla and Native Elements, street dancing, and family activities. Presented by the Civic Joy Fund and SCDC; a second date follows September 25.

events.title: Sunday Streets Excelsior
events.description: The final stop of Sunday Streets SF's 2026 season comes to the Excelsior, transforming neighborhood streets into a car-free community space with free activities, live music, and cultural programming.

moreNews.headline: Gumbo Social Returns August 17 After Six-Week Revamp; Mayor Lurie Visits Third Street
moreNews.body: Bayview's beloved Black-owned soul food restaurant Gumbo Social is set to reopen on August 17 after a planned six-week summer closure that owner Dontaye Ball said was necessary to retool operations and ensure the restaurant's long-term health. "Either we pause for six weeks, or we risk closing in six months," Ball wrote on the restaurant's website. Separately, Mayor Daniel Lurie paid a personal visit to the Third Street corridor last weekend, ordering breakfast from Chef Vanessa Lee's Smoke Soul Kitchen and touring several upcoming businesses, including Lee's forthcoming Chapter 3 bookstore, which has received a grant from the Mayor's Office of Economic and Workforce Development, according to Mission Local.

moreNews.headline: Bayview Oyster Bar Coming to 5114 Third St., Replacing Long-Shuttered Café
moreNews.body: A new modern seafood restaurant called Bayview Oyster Bar is set to open at 5114 Third St. in Bayview–Hunters Point, filling a space that has been vacant since Word. A Cafe shut its doors in 2021 early in the COVID-19 pandemic. The opening would add a much-needed dining option to the Third Street commercial corridor, which has seen a wave of more than 25 new businesses open since 2021, according to Mission Local's Bayview Buzz column.

moreNews.headline: T-Third Muni Platforms Along Third Street Cleaned Up and Repaired
moreNews.body: The SFMTA has completed a two-weekend cleanup and repair of Muni platforms along Third Street in the Bayview, with workers repainting platforms, replacing broken glass, and making other improvements that the agency said had not been made since the T-Third line opened in 2007. The spruced-up stations are part of ongoing investment in the Bayview corridor. The SFMTA's Bayview Community Pathway project — a protected bikeway and pedestrian safety corridor running parallel to Third Street — was approved by the SFMTA Board in December 2025 and is now moving into design.

moreNews.headline: Back-to-School Resource Event at Southeast Community Center This Sunday
moreNews.body: The nonprofit Us4Us is hosting a free backpack giveaway and back-to-school resource fair on Sunday, August 15, from 1:00 to 4:30 p.m. at the Southeast Community Center at 1550 Evans Ave. in Bayview. Backpacks are available for youth entering first through twelfth grade; attendees must register and bring their child. In addition to backpacks and school supplies, families can connect with community organizations and children can enjoy games and activities.

restaurants.name: Excelsior Coffee
restaurants.description: Resident-owned Excelsior café serving espresso drinks, bags of beans to go, and ube pastries; a neighborhood anchor on the Mission Street corridor.

restaurants.name: Tala Wine Bar
restaurants.description: Small natural wine bar in the Excelsior with a long imported wine list and a relaxed, community-centered atmosphere.

restaurants.name: Ty Sandwich
restaurants.description: Excelsior sandwich counter praised for some of San Francisco's best bánh mì, filled with exceptional marinated meats.

restaurants.name: Beijing Restaurant
restaurants.description: Excelsior stalwart running a quick-service, Beijing-focused kitchen with a book-length menu of classic northern Chinese dishes.

restaurants.name: Champa Garden
restaurants.description: One of San Francisco's only Laotian restaurants, serving traditional dishes from Laos in a casual setting on Ocean Avenue.

restaurants.name: Ofena
restaurants.description: Buzzy upscale Italian restaurant in Lakeside Village near Ocean Avenue, serving Italian lunch and dinner using Rize Up Bakery bread for its sandwiches.

restaurants.name: Ocean Ale House
restaurants.description: Homey neighborhood brewery on Ocean Avenue offering craft beers brewed on-site alongside pub food and regular live music.

restaurants.name: Beep's Burgers
restaurants.description: Beloved Ingleside hamburger stand on Ocean Avenue, widely considered one of San Francisco's best burger joints.

restaurants.name: Royal Baking Co.
restaurants.description: Century-old Excelsior bakery on Mission Street, one of six legacy businesses on the corridor that have operated for more than 60 years.

restaurants.name: Smoke Soul Kitchen
restaurants.type: Soul food breakfast and brunch restaurant
restaurants.description: Chef Vanessa Lee's Bayview breakfast and brunch spot on Third Street serving soul food favorites; recently received a mayoral visit and a city grant for her planned Chapter 3 bookstore adjacent to the kitchen.

shops.name: SCRAP — Scroungers' Center for Reusable Art Parts
shops.type: Creative reuse art supply store and workshop space
shops.description: Beloved 50-year-old nonprofit that collects donated overstock paper, fabric, and art materials and redistributes them to artists, educators, and community members; just opened its new permanent 26,000-sq-ft home.

shops.name: Expert Pet
shops.description: Sprawling neighborhood pet store housed in a former bank building on Ocean Avenue, offering supplies and services for a wide range of pets.

shops.name: The Plant Lady SF
shops.description: Recently expanded Ingleside plant boutique on Ocean Avenue that was filled to capacity during a recent weekday visit, testament to its local popularity.

shops.name: Serge a Lot
shops.description: One of San Francisco's last remaining sewing machine repair stores, a longtime Ingleside fixture on Ocean Avenue serving generations of sewists.

artEntertainment.name: Ruth Williams Bayview Opera House
artEntertainment.type: Community performing arts center and theater
artEntertainment.description: San Francisco's oldest community theater and the performing arts and cultural center of the Bayview, currently hosting an open call for artists on the theme 'Art is Resistance: Preserving the Past, Creating the Future.'

artEntertainment.name: India Basin Waterfront Park
artEntertainment.description: The southern half of this landmark 10-acre, $200 million environmental-justice park at 900 Innes Ave. opened in 2024, giving Bayview residents their first direct waterfront access in generations with trails, a food pavilion, and a makers' shop.

artEntertainment.name: Crocker Amazon Playground & Recreation Center
artEntertainment.description: Large Excelsior park featuring a skate park, lighted soccer fields, children's play areas, sport courts, a Hummingbird Farm, and four new pickleball courts opened in 2025; subject of an ongoing $50 million ballfield renovation debate.

artEntertainment.name: John McLaren Park
artEntertainment.description: San Francisco's second-largest park at 317 acres, spanning Visitacion Valley, Excelsior, and Crocker Amazon, offering hiking trails, a lake, picnic areas, and a golf course.
artEntertainment.address: John McLaren Park, San Francisco, CA 94134

gymsRecreation.name: Yoga Flow SF — Ocean Avenue
gymsRecreation.description: Housed in a stunning former Masonic temple, this family-owned studio off Ocean Avenue specializes in heated Vinyasa flow and also offers slow flow, restorative yoga, and a 200-hour teacher training program.

gymsRecreation.name: Excelsior Yoga
gymsRecreation.description: Mission Street studio offering 90-minute classical Hatha yoga classes blended with science and spirituality, with three class levels available; also offers Seifukujutsu bodywork and Reiki energy healing.
gymsRecreation.address: 4610 Mission St, Fl 3, San Francisco, CA 94112

gymsRecreation.name: Bayview YMCA
gymsRecreation.description: Community recreation center in the Bayview offering gym facilities, fitness classes, youth programs, and a kids zone featured at Sunday Streets Bayview.

gymsRecreation.name: Crocker Amazon Pickleball Courts
gymsRecreation.description: Four dedicated pickleball courts at Crocker Amazon Playground, opened in 2025 and available for reservation through SF Rec and Park's online booking system; converted from a volleyball court to meet surging citywide demand.
